article_title: Rewriting the Curriculum: A Systematic Review of Generative AI-Driven Pedagogical Change and Emerging Systems of Learning in Higher Education
citation: Alvedi Sabani, Mohamed H. Farah, Putra Endi Catyanadika, Dian Retno Sari Dewi, Vineet Tawani. (2026). Rewriting the curriculum: A systematic review of generative AI-driven pedagogical change and emerging systems of learning in higher education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100667. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100667
title: 36-study PRISMA systematic review corpus on GenAI in higher education (2023–2025)
description: The final corpus of the PRISMA-guided systematic literature review, screened from 209 Scopus records down to 36 peer-reviewed articles published 2023–2025. The article reports that it "synthesised 36 peer-reviewed studies published between 2023 and 2025, spanning a variety of disciplines including education (n = 16), computer science and IT (n = 6), business and management (n = 5), engineering (n = 3), health sciences (n = 2), and interdisciplinary programs (n = 4)". Most studies focused on undergraduate education (n = 23), with ChatGPT the dominant tool studied.
requirements: Screened via PRISMA 2020 procedures with dual-reviewer title/abstract and full-text screening and MMAT-based quality appraisal
constraints: Screening was not blind to bibliographic information and inter-rater reliability was not quantified
target_learning_goals: synthesis of GenAI integration into curriculum, pedagogy, assessment and institutional change
examples: Geographic distribution: North America (n = 12), Europe (n = 9), Asia-Pacific (n = 9), other regions including Africa and South America (n = 6)
key_sources: Alvedi Sabani, Mohamed H. Farah, Putra Endi Catyanadika, Dian Retno Sari Dewi, Vineet Tawani. (2026). Rewriting the curriculum: A systematic review of generative AI-driven pedagogical change and emerging systems of learning in higher education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100667. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100667

article_title: Perfectionism in Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review
citation: Grugan, M. C., Hill, A. P., Madigan, D. J., Donachie, T. C., Olsson, L. F., & Etherson, M. E. (2021). Perfectionism and Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09597-7
title: Evidence base of 36 studies (N = 10,737) on perfectionism in academically gifted students, 1994–2018
description: The review assembles and catalogues the full empirical evidence base on perfectionism in young academically gifted students: "We identified a total of 36 studies (N = 10,737 students) published over 24 years (1994–2018)". Each study is coded for gifted-identification method, perfectionism measure, design, and outcomes, and appraised with a methodological quality score. Twenty-four studies used a variable-based approach and twelve a group-based approach, organised into achievement, personality, motivation, emotion and well-being, and interpersonal domains.
requirements: Studies must include an empirical examination of perfectionism in students identified as gifted within an educational context, aged under 18, with criterion variables or group comparisons
constraints: Studies vary considerably in how giftedness is operationalised and measured, so the review cautions that "some caution is required when comparing and aggregating findings across the studies"
target_learners: young students identified as academically gifted
target_learning_goals: mapping correlates and consequences of perfectionism in gifted education research
examples: The included studies span the USA, China, Czech Republic, Australia, Canada, the Philippines, and one Japan–USA cross-national study
key_sources: Grugan, M. C., Hill, A. P., Madigan, D. J., Donachie, T. C., Olsson, L. F., & Etherson, M. E. (2021). Perfectionism and Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09597-7

article_title: The potential of 360-degree virtual reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children
citation: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Matthews, B., Simpson, K., Strugnell, G., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2020). The potential of 360-degree Virtual Reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children. https://www.lsv.com.au/vr
title: Use 360° VR videos to teach safety skills for hazardous situations without exposing learners to real danger
description: The article recommends 360° VR videos as a safe way to teach skills for hazardous situations: "it can expose trainees to simulated hazardous situations without putting them in any actual physical danger". The water-safety study demonstrated this by letting children experience beach rip-current hazards virtually. The authors extend this to other hazards children may encounter and to organizations such as museums and water-safety bodies.
requirements: Content designed to address specific hazards relevant to learners, with realistic first-person experience
constraints: The 360° videos used were passive experiences where participants were limited to the role of observers, which the authors note may limit learning benefits relative to more interactive VR
examples: Children watched four 360° beach videos on reading safety signs, spotting a rip current, surviving a rip current, and asking for help, using cardboard headsets and headphones
key_sources: Araiza-Alba, P., Keane, T., Matthews, B., Simpson, K., Strugnell, G., Chen, W. S., & Kaufman, J. (2020). The potential of 360-degree Virtual Reality videos to teach water-safety skills to children. https://www.lsv.com.au/vr

article_title: The effects of communication training on communication competence - a 360° evaluation.
citation: Zöll Lisa, Deschner James, Hollinderbäumer Anke, Nowak Thomas, Zajontz Tamara, Behling Lina, Fischbeck Sabine, Schmidt Uwe, Pfeiffer-Grötz Thekla J. (2025). The effects of communication training on communication competence – a 360° evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07676-9
title: 360° evaluation of communication competence combining student self-assessment with ratings by treatment partners, course tutors and patients
description: A multi-perspective evaluation design in which students' communication competence is assessed not only by the students themselves but also by course tutors, treatment partners and treated patients, using questionnaires derived from a validated self-assessment instrument on five-point Likert scales. The article states such an evaluation "from different perspectives should provide a more objective assessment of the potential of communication training" and that the 360° perspective "provides valuable feedback from all groups of people involved". Questionnaires were pseudonymized with a personal code and administered via EvaSys survey software.
requirements: Good observability of the assessed skills is elementary for external evaluation; the informative value depends heavily on the observational skills of the course tutors and the tutory relationship.
constraints: Accurate and objective assessment is only possible if the rater has known the person long enough, otherwise the first impression is overrated (citing Eichinger et al.); patients could not differentiate between students.
examples: Treatment partners, course tutors and patients were surveyed during the semester; the differentiation of effects decreased across rater groups, from self-assessments to treatment partners to tutors to patients.
key_sources: Zöll Lisa, Deschner James, Hollinderbäumer Anke, Nowak Thomas, Zajontz Tamara, Behling Lina, Fischbeck Sabine, Schmidt Uwe, Pfeiffer-Grötz Thekla J. (2025). The effects of communication training on communication competence – a 360° evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07676-9

article_title: Virtual reality as an engaging and enjoyable method for delivering emergency clinical simulation training: a prospective, interventional study of medical undergraduates.
citation: Walls Risheka, Nageswaran Priyanka, Cowell Adrian, Sehgal Tunav, White Thomas, McVeigh James, Staykov Stefan, Basett Paul, Mitelpunkt Daniel, Sam Amir H. (2024). Virtual reality as an engaging and enjoyable method for delivering emergency clinical simulation training: a prospective, interventional study of medical undergraduates. BMC Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-024-03433-9
title: 360-degree VR emergency simulation scenarios (cardiac arrest and life-threatening asthma)
description: Two 15-minute emergency scenarios, cardiac arrest and life-threatening asthma, created using 360-degree filming of acted-out scenarios and delivered interactively in VR. "Interactivity was introduced with questions and variable scene branching dictated by student responses." Each simulation consisted of a baseline period followed by alternating scenes and questions, with a 20-minute debrief identical in format for both delivery methods. Students experienced each scenario once in VR and once on desktop.
requirements: VR headsets with built-in eye tracking (Pico Neo 3 Pro Eye) and heart rate sensors were used for measurement; scenarios require 360-degree filmed content and branching interactivity
constraints: The 360-degree VR scenarios do not allow training in technical skills, which in-person simulation provides; haptic feedback is described as an evolving field
target_learning_goals: managing medical emergencies such as cardiac arrest and life-threatening asthma
examples: Students in groups of 10-15 experienced both scenarios, randomly assigned to start with cardiac arrest in VR or on desktop, then crossed over to the other modality.
key_sources: Walls Risheka, Nageswaran Priyanka, Cowell Adrian, Sehgal Tunav, White Thomas, McVeigh James, Staykov Stefan, Basett Paul, Mitelpunkt Daniel, Sam Amir H. (2024). Virtual reality as an engaging and enjoyable method for delivering emergency clinical simulation training: a prospective, interventional study of medical undergraduates. BMC Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-024-03433-9

article_title: Impact of a virtual reality-based simulation training for shoulder dystocia on human and technical skills among caregivers: a randomized-controlled trial.
citation: Falcone Veronica, Catic Anja, Heinzl Florian, Steinbauer Philipp, Wagner Michael, Mikula Fanny, Dorittke Tim, Roessler Bernhard, Farr Alex. (2024). Impact of a virtual reality-based simulation training for shoulder dystocia on human and technical skills among caregivers: a randomized-controlled trial. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-57785-6
title: 360°-VR shoulder dystocia scenario video (2 min 50 s, GoPro Max capture, Quest 2 headset)
description: An immersive 360°-VR scenario developed to explore all obstetrical maneuvers needed to manage shoulder dystocia, lasting "2 min and 50 s". It was scripted and approved by obstetrics experts, filmed with a GoPro Max 360 camera placed centrally in the delivery room, and viewed on a standalone Meta Quest 2 headset with 4k resolution at a 75-Hz refresh rate, allowing participants to move freely within the room. The script depicts a G1P0 patient with gestational diabetes at 40+2 weeks whose delivery reveals the turtle sign, walking through the HELP-RER maneuvers including the Gaskin and Wood maneuvers.
requirements: A standalone VR headset such as the Quest 2; no computer connection or additional sensors are needed while still offering wireless connection for a live view
constraints: The 360° technology is non-interactive, providing immersive experience through non-interactive visual and auditory observations, and the training lacked a haptic modality
target_learning_goals: recognizing shoulder dystocia and executing the modified ALSO (HELP-RER) maneuver sequence
examples: The scenario shows the resident physician stopping the oxytocin infusion, calling for help, evaluating episiotomy, performing McRoberts three times, unsuccessful suprapubic pressure, then the roll-onto-all-fours and Wood maneuvers until the shoulder is delivered
key_sources: Falcone Veronica, Catic Anja, Heinzl Florian, Steinbauer Philipp, Wagner Michael, Mikula Fanny, Dorittke Tim, Roessler Bernhard, Farr Alex. (2024). Impact of a virtual reality-based simulation training for shoulder dystocia on human and technical skills among caregivers: a randomized-controlled trial. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-57785-6

article_title: Using Virtual Reality Head-Mounted Displays to Assess Skills in Emergency Medicine: Validity Study.
citation: Marie Høxbro Knudsen, Niklas Breindahl, Tor-Salve Dalsgaard, Dan Isbye, Anne Grethe Mølbak, Gerhard Tiwald, Morten Bo Søndergaard Svendsen, Lars Konge, Joanna Bergström, Tobias Todsen. (2023). Using Virtual Reality Head-Mounted Displays to Assess Skills in Emergency Medicine: Validity Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/45210
title: 360MedQuest VR application: 360-degree video scenarios with integrated MCQs played in a head-mounted display
description: 360MedQuest is a VR application developed in Unity that integrates multiple-choice questions into high-resolution stereoscopic 360-degree videos of full-scale emergency medicine scenarios, played on Oculus Quest head-mounted displays. Each scenario is "one long video sequence paused by an MCQ overlaid onto the video image in VR"; each MCQ has 3 options with a single correct answer, and a narrator's voice reveals the correct answer before the scenario continues. The app was used to assess emergency medicine skills across five scenarios (COVID-19 respiratory distress, trauma and hypovolemic shock, myocardial infarction with cardiac arrest, anaphylaxis, and hypoglycemia).
requirements: A 360-degree video camera and VR head-mounted display hardware; scenarios and MCQs written by a multidisciplinary expert group based on curriculum and relevant guidelines
constraints: MCQs were limited to 1 correct answer out of 3 options, making the design less transferable to real life than full-scale simulation where students can freely make treatment decisions
target_learners: medical students, particularly senior medical students in emergency medicine
target_learning_goals: assessment of emergency medicine diagnostic and treatment decision-making skills
examples: Five emergency scenarios and one introduction scenario were recorded with a Titan 8-lens VR camera at a full-scale simulation room at CAMES, with teachers and students playing patients, relatives, and staff
key_sources: Marie Høxbro Knudsen, Niklas Breindahl, Tor-Salve Dalsgaard, Dan Isbye, Anne Grethe Mølbak, Gerhard Tiwald, Morten Bo Søndergaard Svendsen, Lars Konge, Joanna Bergström, Tobias Todsen. (2023). Using Virtual Reality Head-Mounted Displays to Assess Skills in Emergency Medicine: Validity Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/45210

article_title: A Training Intervention through a 360° Multisource Feedback Model.
citation: Sureda Elena, Chacón-Moscoso Salvador, Sanduvete-Chaves Susana, Sesé Albert. (2021). A Training Intervention through a 360° Multisource Feedback Model. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18179137
title: 360° Multisource Feedback (MSF) model for evaluating nontechnical professional competencies
description: The 360° MSF model evaluates professional performance by triangulating multiple rater sources familiar with the role: "supervisors, co-workers, and the workers themselves (self-assessment)". Competencies are operationalized into behavioral indicators rated on a shared 10-point Likert-type scale divided into five levels, and all assessments are compared to obtain an overall performance score. The article applies it in nine phases over three years to evaluate whether a training intervention changed hospital professionals' nontechnical competencies, arguing triangulation lets each source's strengths compensate for others' weaknesses.
requirements: Raters must have direct information and knowledge about the person assessed, with enough information to evaluate real behavior
All raters should use a single Likert-type scale to facilitate comparisons and consensus
The professional to be evaluated should participate in the rater selection process
constraints: Not adequate for assessing specific or technical competencies, because co-workers often lack direct observation of job performance
Logistical complexity of establishing assessment circuits and the lack of an evaluative culture reduce optimal functioning
target_learners: health professionals in postgraduate training and professional development
target_learning_goals: nontechnical transversal competencies such as teamwork, adaptability, commitment, results orientation, and leadership
examples: The model was implemented in nine phases over 2016–2018, from management commitment and protocol development through pretest, training, posttest, and personalized feedback reports
key_sources: Sureda Elena, Chacón-Moscoso Salvador, Sanduvete-Chaves Susana, Sesé Albert. (2021). A Training Intervention through a 360° Multisource Feedback Model. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18179137
